newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania leu trend uncertain despite resolve.
newsitem.headline: Romania leu trend uncertain despite resolve.

text.p: The trend for Romania's leu currency in coming months remains unclear despite official pledges to keep it from strengthening and implement current account convertibility, analysts said on Friday.

Analysts say exchange rate moves depended on interest rates levels, traditional pre-winter pressure on the currency and the pace of structural reforms which would determine foreign investors' interest in Romania.
Central bank governor Mugur Isarescu said on Thursday at the close of a month-long International Monetary Fund mission assessing reforms that Romania could not afford a strong leu.

And Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea said Romania would achieve current account convertibility by September as the currency had stabilised in recent months near 7,500 to the dollar after a record low of about 9,000 in March.

The IMF praised Romania's achievements in reducing monthly inflation to a record low of 0.7 percent in July, in boosting foreign exchange reserves and in producing an amended budget that kept social programmes intact. But the Fund was less pleased with restructuring top-heavy communist-era industry.
Analysts said the real test for both the leu and reforms could still lie ahead.
"So far all achievements have been based on monetary and financial steps and not on fundamentals," said one trader.
"Attention must now focus on the pace of structural steps combined with patience of ordinary people in helping preserve stability and keeping reforms on track."
Further foreign capital inflows, which flooded Romania in recent months, would help reduce any pressure on the leu.
Retail traders said current account convertibility would mean changing rules limiting purchases of foreign currency by Romanian individuals to the equivalent of $500 per year.
"This will boost competition between retail houses and also be a blow up for black market traders," said Dan Simionescu, manager of IDM Exchange in Bucharest.
Analysts said other moves would be needed to avoid capital outflows through cash deals on the retail market. Authorities would also have to monitor money laundering.
"I think they (the government) still has to choose whether to give up the limit or set a higher one at, say $3,000 per year, for a while," said another trader.
Pressure on the leu traditionally builds in Romania in autumn from increased fuel imports and psychological fears of a run on the currency.
Bankers said that removing the $500 limit was unlikely to put great pressure on the leu, but warned that monetary policies should be cautious to avoid undermining confidence.
"If people perceive deposit rates as being unattractive, they will rush to buy hard currency," he said. "That's why it's vital to achieve a soft landing in interest rates."
Though lower than a few months ago, banks' deposit rates, now at about an annual 45 percent, still offered good returns.
